**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks, a silent metronome counting down the seconds until I must begin. A thousand words—a vast expanse, yet so finite. What do I fill it with? The weight of expectation presses against my ribs, a quiet insistence that these words must mean *something*.

I think of the ocean first. Not the postcard version, all turquoise and gentle waves, but the real one—the one that roars and swallows ships whole. The one that carries secrets in its depths, bones and lost treasures and the whispers of drowned sailors. A thousand words could describe the ocean, but never capture it. Not really.

Then there’s the city at night. Neon signs flicker like dying stars, and the streets hum with the low thrum of engines and laughter. A woman in a red coat walks past, her heels clicking against wet pavement. She doesn’t look back. A thousand words could follow her, but where would she go? What story would she tell?

I remember a conversation I had once, in a café that smelled of cinnamon and old books. A stranger told me about the time he got lost in the mountains. He spoke of the cold, the way the wind carved through his jacket like a knife, how the silence was so thick it felt like drowning. He said he thought he was going to die. Then, just as the sun began to set, he found a path. A thousand words could retrace his steps, but would they carry the same fear? The same relief?

Words are strange things. They build bridges and burn them. They can be weapons or blankets, shields or arrows. A thousand of them could be a novel, a manifesto, a love letter. Or they could be nothing at all—just noise, just static, just the sound of fingers tapping against a keyboard in an empty room.

I think of the first time I understood that words had power. I was eight, and I called my best friend a name I didn’t fully understand. His face crumpled, and I realized, with a sickening lurch, that I had hurt him. That I could hurt him. A thousand words could apologize, but some wounds don’t heal that way.

There’s a tree outside my window. It’s old, its branches gnarled and twisted like arthritic fingers. Birds nest in its hollows, and sometimes, when the wind is right, it creaks like an old ship. A thousand words could describe its bark, its leaves, the way the light filters through its canopy. But would they make you see it? Would they make you care?

I wonder if anyone will read these words. If they do, will they hear my voice in them? Or will they just be ink on a page, pixels on a screen—something to skim and forget?

A thousand words. I’ve used nearly half. The rest could be about anything—the taste of salt on skin after swimming, the way my grandmother’s hands shook when she threaded a needle, the exact shade of blue the sky turns just before a storm. But time is running out, and the cursor still blinks, patient and indifferent.

So I’ll end here, with this: words are never just words. They’re echoes, fingerprints, ghosts. A thousand of them can change a life—or pass by like a breath.

And now, mine are spent.
